question: If one of our farmers uses a banned pesticide, they face a six-month prison sentence and are fined EUR 150 000 plus 10% of their turnover. However, the same penalties do not apply to those who import agricultural products from North African countries that use dichloropropene. Tomato exports from Morocco to Europe have increased by 52% in 10 years.

Citrus fruit, tomatoes and potatoes are imported from North Africa, Türkiye, Morocco, Tunisia and Egypt. Likewise, genetically modified products from the US or Canadian products with traces of glyphosate are imported in an ironic act of discrimination that is insulting to our producers and consumers.

Consequently, at the same time as it proposes greening European agriculture, the Commission foresees a 22% drop in production in the EU by 2035. For instance, in Greece, in the 11-month period of 2023, imports of fruit and vegetables totalled 601.18 thousand tonnes compared to 506.686 thousand tonnes during the same period in 2022. That is an 18.65% increase in one year.
Greek products now account for nearly 50% of products in Greek shops while just a few years ago they accounted for around 70%. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What steps does it plan to take to ensure strict compliance of imports with European production standards?
Assuming it recognises the signs of inadequate checks being carried out on illegal imports, what must the Member States do to stop these?
Are there any recommendations on this matter that are not followed by Greece?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.5.2024) The food safety for European consumers is a priority for the Commission. Food products placed on the EU market, regardless of their origin, must comply with Maximum Residue Levels (MRLs) for pesticides. Member States monitor compliance with MRLs based on an EU-coordinated multi-annual control programme1 and risk-based national control programmes2.

Their results are published3 by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). According to its report for 20214 Greece analysed 3,658 samples for pesticide residues, 726 originated in third countries. Of those, 87% contained no residues or traces below the MRLs. 7% of samples were noncompliant for which Greece took appropriate enforcement action, e.g.

, products were removed from the EU market and the competent authorities of the country of origin of the product were requested to take corrective actions to address the irregularities identified. These results are consistent with the overall rate of 6.4% of non-compliances identified for 19,053 samples analysed in the EU in 2021 for pesticide residues.

The Commission performs audits both in Member States on import controls, and in third countries exporting goods to the EU, to establish if their official control systems can ensure compliance of goods intended for export to the EU with applicable EU rules. The reports of those audits are published, including the actions taken to address the reports’ recommendations.
These actions are followed up by the Commission on a regular basis.
